title: Hooks that help instead of blocking
summary: post-checkout, post-merge and post-commit cannot reject anything — they run after the fact. Use them to fix the small annoyances: stale dependencies after a branch switch, and a reminder when a lockfile changes.
mental_model: Hooks split into two families. The `pre-` ones gate an operation and can refuse it. The `post-` ones run afterwards, cannot stop anything, and exist purely to automate what a human would otherwise forget.

steps.title: The annoyance
steps.why: Switching to a branch that changed requirements.txt leaves your installed packages out of date. Nothing warns you; the app just fails at import time twenty minutes later.

steps.title: Write a post-checkout hook
steps.why: It receives the previous HEAD, the new HEAD, and a flag: 1 for a branch switch, 0 for a file checkout. Diffing those two shas tells you exactly which files changed underneath you.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Warn when a branch switch changes dependency files.

prev="$1"
new="$2"
branch_switch="$3"

[ "$branch_switch" = "1" ] || exit 0
[ "$prev" = "$new" ] && exit 0

changed=$(git diff --name-only "$prev" "$new" 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'requirements.txt|package-lock.json|go.sum|Gemfile.lock')

if [ -n "$changed" ]; then
  echo "----------------------------------------------"
  echo "post-checkout: dependency files changed:"
  echo "$changed" | sed 's/^/  /'
  echo "post-checkout: run your install command before testing."
  echo "----------------------------------------------"
  git diff --stat "$prev" "$new" -- $changed
fi

exit 0

steps.title: Switch branches and watch it fire
steps.why: The hook prints its warning as part of the checkout output. It cannot block anything — a post hook's exit code is ignored — which is why it is safe to be chatty.
steps.expect: The dependency warning printed on the way in and again on the way out.

steps.title: Add a post-merge hook for the same reason
steps.why: `git pull` changes your dependencies just as often as a branch switch does. post-merge takes one argument — whether it was a squash merge — and `HEAD@{1}` is where you were before it.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Same warning, for merges and pulls.

changed=$(git diff --name-only HEAD@{1} HEAD 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'requirements.txt|package-lock.json|go.sum')

if [ -n "$changed" ]; then
  echo "post-merge: dependencies changed in this merge:"
  echo "$changed" | sed 's/^/  /'
  echo "post-merge: reinstall before running anything."
fi

exit 0

steps.expect: The merge succeeds and the hook reports the dependency change.

verify.label: the merge brought the new dependencies in

steps.title: post-commit, for a local reminder
steps.why: It runs after the commit exists, so it cannot change or reject it. Useful for recording what you did — here, appending to a local scratch log that is never committed.

write.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Append every commit to a local, untracked worklog.

printf '%s  %s\n' "$(git log -1 --format=%h)" "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" >> .git/worklog.txt
echo "post-commit: logged $(git log -1 --format=%h) to .git/worklog.txt"
exit 0

from prometheus_client import Counter

DOSES = Counter('doses_total', 'Doses delivered')

verify.label: the post-commit hook recorded the commit
verify.hint: post-commit runs after the commit object exists

steps.title: Prove a post hook cannot block
steps.why: Give post-commit a non-zero exit and commit again. Git prints nothing about it and the commit stands — post hooks are advisory by design, so a broken one cannot wedge your repository.
steps.expect: The hook fails loudly and the commit is created anyway.

verify.label: the failing post hook did not block the commit

steps.title: Share the useful ones
steps.why: Same mechanism as always: track them and set `core.hooksPath`. Automation that only exists on your machine is a personal preference, not a team practice.

verify.label: the dependency-warning hooks are shared with the team
verify.hint: copy them into .githooks, commit, set core.hooksPath

verify.label: a failing post hook could not block a commit
verify.hint: post hooks' exit codes are ignored by design

verify.label: hooks come from the tracked directory

pitfalls: post-checkout also fires for `git checkout -- <file>`. Check the third argument is 1, or your hook runs constantly.
post-merge cannot tell you what a rebase did — rebase fires post-checkout instead, once per replayed commit in some versions.
Never run an installer automatically from a hook. Tell the human what changed; silently mutating someone's environment is worse than the stale dependency.
post hooks' exit codes are ignored. If you need to block something, you need a `pre-` hook.
Anything written under `.git/` is never committed and never cloned — fine for a personal worklog, useless for anything shared.
cheatsheet: after a checkout or branch switch
after amend or rebase rewrites commits
